chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, all from Ibn Mahboub, from Ibn Ra'ib, from Humran ibn Ayn, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a young slave-girl who had not yet reached adulthood, being seven years old, who was with a man and a woman. The man claimed that she was his owned slave-girl, and the woman claimed that she was her daughter. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'Ali (peace be upon him) had judged regarding this.' I said, 'And what did Ali (peace be upon him) judge regarding this?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'He (peace be upon him) used to say: All people are free, except for the one who confesses upon himself with slavery, and he is an adult, and the one upon whom the proof is established by the one who claims. So if witnesses testify that she is his owned slave-girl, and it is not known that she was sold or gifted, I would hand over the slave-girl to him, until the woman establishes one who testifies for her that the slave-girl is her daughter, free like her. So she should be handed over to her, and taken out from the hand of the man.' I said, 'So if the man does not establish witnesses that she is his owned slave-girl?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'She would be taken out from his hand. So if the woman establishes the proof that she is her daughter, she would be handed over to her. And if the man does not establish the proof upon what he claims, and the woman does not establish the proof upon what she claims, the way of the slave-girl would be left open. She can go wherever she so desires.'
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on a disputed slave-girl when neither the owner nor the mother can provide conclusive proof?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the foundational Shia legal principle of 'al-aslu al-bar'ah' (presumption of freedom), where the default status of a human is liberty unless proven otherwise through specific evidence or self-admission. It illustrates the procedural burden of proof, requiring the claimant of ownership to produce witnesses confirming the slave's status, while the mother must prove her lineage to reclaim her daughter, reflecting the Imams' application of Ali ibn Abi Talib’s jurisprudence. The ruling ensures that in the absence of conclusive evidence from either party, the girl is released, emphasizing the high threshold for maintaining the state of servitude.
